fields.title: Fiche d’information MSNA 2026 - Évaluation multisectorielle des besoins Zone à accessibilité limitée, Province d’ Ituri, République Démocratique du Congo (RDC)
fields.body:
**Zone de santé de Bambu, Bunia, Damas, Nia Nia, Fataki, Kilo, Mandiba, Mangala, Mongbalu, Nizi, Nyankundé et Rwanpara**  
**Province d’ Ituri, République Démocratique du Congo (RDC)**

**CONTEXTE**

L’est de la RDC reste marqué par une crise humanitaire prolongée et complexe, caractérisée par des déplacements croissants et des besoins humanitaires importants. En 2026, plus de 3,2 millions de personnes sont confrontées à une insécurité alimentaire aiguë de niveau urgence (phase 4 de l’IPC), tandis que les capacités de réponse demeurent insuffisantes. Les déplacements, la perte des moyens d’existence, les difficultés d’accès aux services essentiels et les contraintes sécuritaires et logistiques aggravent les vulnérabilités et limitent l’accès humanitaire ainsi que la disponibilité de données fiables. Afin de contribuer à combler ces lacunes informationnelles, REACH met en œuvre en 2026 une Évaluation multisectorielle des besoins (MSNA) dans les cinq provinces de l’est de la RDC dont Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Maniema et Tanganyika. Cette évaluation vise à fournir des données récentes, fiables, robustes et comparables sur la nature et la sévérité des besoins humanitaires, au niveau des zones de santé, afin d’alimenter l’Aperçu des besoins humanitaires (HNO) et le cycle de programmation humanitaire (HPC) 2027. Sa méthodologie est détaillée dans les [Termes de références](https://repository.impact-initiatives.org/document/impact/34e8a812/DRC2603_MSNA_TDR_2026_version-finale.pdf) et les produits d’information liés à ce projet sont disponibles sur le [Centre de Ressources](https://www.impact-initiatives.org/resource-centre/?category%5B%5D=information_products&category%5B%5D=data_methods&location%5B%5D=609&order=latest&limit=10).

fields.title: République Démocratique du Congo: Aperçu de situation - Évaluation des impacts de la montée des eaux du lac Tanganyika le long de l’axe Uvira-Nundu, Septembre 2026
fields.body:
**1. Contexte**

Le lac Tanganyika, dans l’est de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC), a connu d’importantes évolutions ces dernières années. Les observations satellitaires documentent une hausse significative du niveau des eaux du lac Tanganyika à partir de 2019, suivie, dès 2020, d’inondations étendues, de la submersion de zones riveraines et d’impacts sur les zones urbaines et les zones humides le long des rives nord du lac. Cette récente montée du niveau des eaux a notamment été associée à une augmentation des précipitations dans le bassin du lac Tanganyika, y compris à une hausse significative des précipitations dans le sousbassin de la Malagarasi. Des niveaux d’eau inhabituellement élevés ont également été observés dans plusieurs Grands Lacs d’Afrique de l’Est depuis 2019-2020.

Bien que des recherches supplémentaires soient nécessaires pour déterminer plus précisément la contribution du changement climatique à ces tendances, les recherches montrent que les variations de température et de circulation atmosphérique au-dessus de l’océan Indien peuvent interagir avec des phénomènes climatiques tels qu’El Niño et contribuer, certaines années, à des précipitations exceptionnellement abondantes et à une hausse du niveau des Grands Lacs de la région. En particulier, des conditions plus chaudes dans l’ouest de l’océan Indien ont été associées à une plus forte convergence de l’humidité et à une augmentation des précipitations en Afrique de l’Est . Des études et des experts régionaux ont également identifié des facteurs non climatiques susceptibles de contribuer à la hausse du niveau des eaux ou de l’aggraver, notamment la déforestation et les changements d’utilisation des terres, l’augmentation de l’érosion et de la sédimentation, ainsi que les constructions non planifiées le long des cours d’eau. En particulier, l’Autorité du lac Tanganyika a indiqué que l’accumulation de sédiments et les constructions autour de la rivière Lukuga ont contribué au rétrécissement de son lit, ce qui pourrait limiter la capacité du seul exutoire de surface du lac Tanganyika à évacuer l’excès d’eau.

Le long de la rive nord-ouest du lac Tanganyika, entre Uvira et Nundu, la montée du niveau des eaux et les aléas hydrologiques ont des implications socio-économiques importantes. Le transport lacustre joue un rôle important dans la connectivité de la zone, reliant les principaux centres urbains, notamment Uvira et Baraka, aux localités plus petites situées le long du lac. Il permet à la fois la circulation de marchandises provenant de l’extérieur de la région et des échanges à plus petite échelle de produits agricoles et halieutiques locaux. Dans un contexte où les infrastructures de transport terrestre restent peu développées et où certains axes routiers sont difficilement praticables, le transport lacustre constitue ainsi une composante importante du système régional de transport et de commerce. Le port Kalundu d’Uvira constitue un nœud important reliant la rive congolaise aux routes commerciales régionales, notamment vers Bujumbura au Burundi et Mpulungu en Zambie.

Bien que l’élévation des eaux du lac ne constitue pas une situation d’urgence, sa récente montée progressive a des répercussions, dont les effets se manifestent après plusieurs années. Ceux-ci sont exacerbés par les fluctuations saisonnières des eaux et les épisodes plus intenses d’inondation, d’érosion et de fortes vagues. Cette distinction est importante pour comprendre les impacts le long de l’axe Uvira-Nundu, les communautés pouvant être confrontées non seulement à des perturbations temporaires pendant les périodes de niveaux d’eau particulièrement élevés, mais également à un empiètement à plus long terme sur les zones habitées, les infrastructures et les espaces économiques.

Dans ce contexte, REACH et Popoli Fratelli DRC ont mené une évaluation environnementale à partir d’une méthodologie mixte. Cette évaluation regroupe des enquêtes réalisées auprès de ménages de villages exposés à la montée des eaux du lac, d’acteurs du marché, des entretiens avec des informateurs clés, des observations de terrain, une cartographie des infrastructures, et une analyse d’images satellitaires. L’évaluation visait à documenter la nature et l’étendue spatiale des aléas hydrologiques affectant les communautés riveraines du lac et leurs répercussions sur la mobilité, l’accès au logement et aux services essentiels, les moyens de subsistance et les chaînes d’approvisionnement des populations. Elle visait également à examiner les stratégies et comportements d’adaptation mis en œuvre au niveau individuel et communautaire ainsi que les priorités en matière de réduction des risques à plus long terme.

fields.title: Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #14 (October 13, 2026)
fields.body:
**FAST FACTS**

- On May 15, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain.
- As of October 11, 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 confirmed deaths had been reported in the DRC.
- On October 5, a case of imported EVD was confirmed in Kenya. The patient had traveled from the DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he died.
- No EVD cases have been confirmed in South Sudan or the Central African Republic, but risk of cross-border transmission remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC.
- In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, but cases have also been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi and Tshopo provinces, indicating an uncontrolled spread of the disease.
- Uganda has officially declared its outbreak to be over, though preparedness activities continue.

**OUR RESPONSE**

- Across the region, our teams are providing case management, infection prevention and control, screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement, training and preparedness planning.
- We are helping more than 110 facilities screen, identify and treat EVD.
- Our supported sites in the DRC have conducted more than 1 million EVD screenings and provided treatment to 2,806 patients, including 828 confirmed cases.
- We have so far trained 6,451 people in the DRC on EVD case management, response and transmission prevention.

With the support of the US Department of State, DG ECHO and other donors, International Medical Corps teams in the DRC, South Sudan and Uganda are actively responding to the outbreak and collaborating closely with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen IPC in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols.

fields.title: Afrique de l’Ouest et centrale : Derniers événements en bref (du 6 au 12 octobre 2026)
fields.body:
**Nigéria**  
*L'épidémie de diphtérie fait 700 morts dans 26 États*

Entre janvier et début octobre 2026, le Nigéria a enregistré plus de 26 000 cas suspects de diphtérie, dont 19 000 infections confirmées et 700 décès dans 26 États, avec un taux de létalité de 3,6 pour cent. Bauchi, Borno, Kano, Katsina et Sokoto représentent 66 pour cent des cas signalés. La surpopulation et l’accès limité aux services essentiels augmentent les risques de transmission, en particulier dans les zones touchées par les conflits et les déplacements. Malgré les efforts de vaccination et de surveillance en cours, la pénurie d’antitoxine diphtérique, les capacités limitées des laboratoires et les retards dans les rapports continuent de limiter la riposte.

**Afrique de l'Ouest**  
*La crise des déplacements s'aggrave alors que près de 4 millions de personnes restent déracinées*

Le HCR a averti que près de 4 millions de personnes sont déplacées au Burkina Faso, au Mali et au Niger, soit près du double du nombre enregistré en 2020. L'insécurité persistante et la violence armée continuent de provoquer des déplacements, exerçant une pression croissante sur les communautés d'accueil, les services essentiels, les ressources en eau et les moyens de subsistance. La crise touche de plus en plus les pays côtiers d’Afrique de l’Ouest, avec des centaines de milliers de personnes cherchant refuge au Bénin, en Côte d’Ivoire, au Ghana et au Togo. Le HCR a appelé à des investissements urgents pour répondre aux besoins humanitaires croissants et renforcer la résilience dans la région.

**République centrafricaine**  
*De fortes pluies et des vents violents affectent 1 400 personnes dans la préfecture du Mbomou*

Depuis le 7 octobre, de fortes pluies et des vents violents ont endommagé des maisons, des latrines communautaires, des puits et des stocks alimentaires à Bakouma et Nzako, dans le sud-est de la République centrafricaine. Au 11 octobre, les évaluations préliminaires indiquent que 280 abris et environ 1 400 personnes ont été touchés. Les familles dont les maisons ont été détruites sont hébergées chez des voisins dans des conditions difficiles. OCHA continue de surveiller la situation et de coordonner une réponse multisectorielle.

**République démocratique du Congo**  
*L’épidémie d’Ebola aggrave la crise humanitaire*

L’épidémie actuelle d’Ebola aggrave une crise humanitaire déjà grave, avec plus de 6,1 millions de personnes déplacées, plus de 26 millions confrontées à l’insécurité alimentaire et plus de 4 millions d’enfants de moins de cinq ans touchés par la malnutrition. L’épidémie se propage parmi les communautés déjà touchées par le conflit, l’insécurité et l’accès perturbé aux services essentiels. Le coordonnateur humanitaire, Damien Mama, a averti que les crises qui se chevauchent aggravent les vulnérabilités et mettent encore plus à rude épreuve les efforts de réponse. Les opérations humanitaires restent difficiles, avec huit travailleurs humanitaires tués depuis le début de 2026. L’ONU et les partenaires humanitaires continuent de fournir une aide vitale, appelant à un soutien international urgent pour répondre aux besoins croissants.

fields.title: West and Central Africa: Latest Events at a glance (6–12 October 2026)
fields.body:
**Nigeria**  
*Diphtheria outbreak claims 700 lives across 26 states*

Between January and early October 2026, Nigeria recorded over 26,000 suspected diphtheria cases, including 19,000 confirmed infections and 700 deaths across 26 states, with a case fatality rate of 3.6 per cent. Bauchi, Borno, Kano, Katsina and Sokoto account for 66 per cent of reported cases. Overcrowding and limited access to essential services increase transmission risks, particularly in conflict- and displacement-affected areas. Despite ongoing vaccination and surveillance efforts, shortages of diphtheria antitoxin, limited laboratory capacity and reporting delays continue to constrain the response.

**West Africa**  
*Displacement crisis deepens as nearly 4 million people remain uprooted*

UNHCR has warned that nearly 4 million people are displaced across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, almost double the number recorded in 2020. Persistent insecurity and armed violence continue to drive displacement, placing growing pressure on host communities, essential services, water resources and livelihoods. The crisis is increasingly affecting coastal West African countries, with hundreds of thousands of people seeking refuge in Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Togo. UNHCR has called for urgent investment to address rising humanitarian needs and strengthen resilience across the region.

**Central African Republic**  
*Heavy rains and strong winds affect 1,400 people in Mbomou Prefecture*

Since 7 October, heavy rains and strong winds have damaged homes, community latrines, wells and food stocks in Bakouma and Nzako, in southeastern Central African Republic. As of 11 October, preliminary assessments indicate that 280 shelters and approximately 1,400 people have been affected. Families whose homes were destroyed are sheltering with neighbours under difficult conditions. OCHA continues to monitor the situation and coordinate a multisectoral response.

**Democratic Republic of the Congo**  
*Ebola outbreak compounds worsening humanitarian crisis*

The ongoing Ebola outbreak is exacerbating an already severe humanitarian crisis, with more than 6.1 million people displaced, over 26 million facing food insecurity and more than 4 million children under five affected by malnutrition. The outbreak is spreading among communities already affected by conflict, insecurity and disrupted access to essential services. Humanitarian Coordinator Damien Mama warned that the overlapping crises are compounding vulnerabilities and further straining response efforts. Humanitarian operations remain challenging, with eight aid workers killed since the beginning of 2026. The UN and humanitarian partners continue to provide life-saving assistance, calling for urgent international support to address growing needs.

fields.title: Central African Republic: Humanitarian Dashboard - Inter-Sectoral Response (January - July 2026)
fields.body:
**HUMANITARIAN SITUATION**

Between January and July 2026, the humanitarian situation in the Central African Republic remained critical. Of the 2.3 million people in need, 1.3 million were targeted under the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP). Only 471,600 people (36 per cent) received at least one form of assistance, while 187,000 people (15 per cent) benefited from adequate multisectoral coverage.  
 Among the 932,100 hyper-prioritized individuals, who represent the most vulnerable populations, only 160,500 people (17 per cent) were reached, leaving 772,000 people without a sufficient response.  
 As of 31 August, US$208.3 million had been mobilized, representing 43.7 per cent of the required funding, leaving a funding gap of US$148.7 million.  
 These results should, however, be interpreted with caution due to significant reporting gaps. Several clusters, including Education, Child Protection, Shelter/NFI (Non-Food Items), CCCM (Camp Coordination and Camp Management), and Protection, did not submit all their data within the required timeframe. This may lead to an underestimation of achievements.

fields.title: Kwango: In Popokabaka, cholera spreads as access to safe water remains limited
fields.body:
**While the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is facing an outbreak of Ebola virus disease in the east of the country, cholera continues to spread in other regions, where limited access to safe water and sanitation infrastructure is contributing to transmission of the disease.**

Since June this year, a cholera outbreak has been affecting the Popokabaka health zone, in DRC’s Kwango province. As of 22 July, 345 suspected cases and 21 deaths were reported across 26 of the health zone’s 35 health areas, representing a case fatality rate of 6.1 per cent. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is supporting the Ministry of Health in the response, including through patient care, epidemiological surveillance, and water, sanitation and hygiene activities.

The outbreak in Popokabaka was officially declared on 25 June, after the National Institute of Biomedical Research confirmed the presence of *Vibrio cholerae*. The three health areas in the provincial capital – Secteur Popo, Cité Popo 1 and Cité Popo 2 – accounted for 200 cases, or 58 per cent of all reported cases.

Considering the potential spread of the disease, MSF deployed an emergency team to support the health authorities in the response. The team is supporting medical care at Popokabaka General Referral Hospital, where a cholera treatment centre has been established to provide care for patients with severe forms of the disease.

Four treatment units have also been set up in four health areas to bring care closer to communities, alongside 31 oral rehydration points providing faster treatment for patients showing symptoms. Since the beginning of the intervention, 450 patients have received care, including 175 at Popokabaka General Referral Hospital.

**Treatment alone is not enough**

Rapid treatment is essential to prevent patients’ conditions from deteriorating and reduce the risk of death. But healthcare alone cannot end a cholera outbreak. In Popokabaka, as the disease continues to spread, access to safe water remains limited, while hygiene and sanitation conditions remain inadequate. A significant proportion of the population relies on rivers for their daily water needs.

According to an assessment conducted by MSF, 61 per cent of the population has access to less than 15 litres of safe water per person per day, the minimum requirement in humanitarian emergencies, according to the World Health Organization. Only 38 per cent have access to functional latrines, while open defecation remains widespread.

These conditions increase the risk of water sources becoming contaminated and facilitate the transmission of cholera, which is primarily spread through the consumption of contaminated water or food.

“We can treat a patient with cholera, rehydrate them and save their life. But if, once they return home, they still do not have access to safe water or latrines, there is a very real risk that the disease will continue to spread,” explains Dr Materne Cirimuanua, medical lead for the Popokabaka response.

The outbreak is taking place in a fragile humanitarian context, marked in particular by violence linked to the Mobondo crisis in western DRC, in which intercommunal conflict has forced many people to flee their homes. This has been compounded by overlapping population movements, including the arrival of more than 2,000 Congolese people expelled from Angola.

As the rainy season approaches, the risk of contamination of water sources could increase further. Heavy rainfall can contribute to the contamination of water points if sanitation infrastructure is inadequate or water sources are not sufficiently protected.

To address this risk and improve access to safe water, MSF has established 36 chlorination points. However, these measures are not enough to meet the population’s needs. Additional efforts and better coordination between the different organisations involved are needed to provide sustainable solutions to water, sanitation and hygiene needs.

“The rainy season can make the situation even more difficult when water sources are not adequately protected and sanitation infrastructure is limited,” Materne says. “Action is needed now to reduce the risks, strengthen access to safe water and bring healthcare services closer to the communities that need them.”

**A response that must reach communities**

Access to healthcare is another major challenge. The Popokabaka health zone has 35 health areas but only one general referral hospital. Some communities can only be reached by canoe, motorcycle or on foot, which can delay access to care for people needing medical attention.

MSF’s emergency team has therefore sought to bring care closer to people living in the worst-affected areas, including by setting up cholera treatment units. At the same time, the team is supporting epidemiological surveillance to monitor the evolution of the outbreak and rapidly identify new hotspots.

Within communities, community health workers and health promoters are also raising awareness about cholera prevention measures and the importance of good hygiene practices.

“In an area where access to safe water remains limited and some communities are difficult to reach, containing the outbreak will require a coordinated response combining healthcare, surveillance, safe water, sanitation and prevention,” Materne says.

“In the context of Popokabaka, MSF calls on health authorities and other stakeholders involved in the response to strengthen their efforts to sustainably improve access to safe water and sanitation, thereby reducing the risk of new cholera outbreaks.” ​

fields.title: ACAPS Briefing Note: Democratic Republic of Congo - Mpox outbreak affecting Kasaï province (13 October 2025)
fields.body:
**CRISIS IMPACT OVERVIEW**

• On 16 September 2026, provincial authorities announced an mpox outbreak in Kasaï province, initially covering five health zones (7Sur7.cd 17/09/2026; mediacongo. net 17/09/2026). By 1 October, 1,017 cases and more than 24 deaths had been reported across all 18 of the province’s health zones (Actualite.cd 01/10/2026).

• The declaration of a provincial mpox outbreak in Kasaï comes five months after the Government announced the end of a national mpox emergency designation; on 2 April, the Government announced a shift from emergency response to resilience, promoting community vigilance given the risk of resurgence (MSPHP 08/04/2026). The end of the emergency designation did not mean that transmission had ceased throughout the country, and available reporting does not establish whether the Kasaï outbreak is a result of continued local transmission or a new introduction into the province.

• Earlier media reporting from 1–2 September quoting health sources identified Kambangoma and Mukwandjanga in Luebo health zone as the main affected locations, approximately 20km from the health zone coordination office. Authorities in Luebo were awaiting laboratory results from the National Biomedical Research Institute, indicating reliance on diagnostic support outside the health zone at that stage (ACP 01/09/2026; Radio Okapi 02/09/2026). The sources reviewed do not establish whether provincial testing arrangements have subsequently changed.

• Hospital staff reported limited equipment and response resources from the outset. Suspected cases included infants aged two to three months. There were also reports of concerns about obtaining food and lodging during hospital care discouraging patients from seeking treatment (ACP 01/09/2026).

• On 4 October, national health authorities deployed Rapid Intervention Teams to Tshikapa to support the Kasaï Provincial Health Division, particularly in Luebo. The mission focuses on epidemiological surveillance, the investigation and early detection of suspected cases, case management, and community awareness, while also reinforcing the operational capacity of local health teams (CongoCroissance 05/10/2026).

• Kasaï is facing a simultaneous measles outbreak and suspected cases of yellow fever, increasing pressure on surveillance and health response capacity (WHO 31/08/2026; Beto 23/09/2026). At 9 October, no cases of Ebola had been reported in the province (CDC 09/10/2026).

• On 26 September, an mpox case was confirmed in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province; by 29 September, there were five confirmed cases reported in Rwampara and Aru health zones of the province (MedAfrik Info Instagram 26/09/2026; mediacongo. net 01/10/2026; Reuters 25/09/2026). Earlier reports dating from July indicate nearly 4,000 cases confirmed in Sud-Kivu since the start of the year (mediacongo.net 23/07/2026). The available reporting does not establish whether cases in Ituri, Kasaï, and Sud-Kivu are linked to the same transmission chains.

fields.title: RDC : Rapport evaluation de la reponse en Sante Sexuelle et Reproductive (SSR) au premier semestre 2026 (avril - mai 2026) [EN/FR]
fields.body:
**ZONE DE SANTE : MASISI - MWESO - BIRAMBIZO - BAMBO - RUTSHURU - KIBIRIZI - BINZA - BENI - BUTEMBO - KATWA**

**Contexte exécutif et aperçu de l'évaluation**

La région orientale de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC), en particulier la province du Nord-Kivu, est confrontée à une crise humanitaire aiguë provoquée par des conflits armés et de graves déplacements de population impliquant plus de 2,5 millions de personnes déplacées internes (PDI). Cet environnement volatile a entraîné une forte augmentation de la mortalité maternelle dans toute la province. Les décès maternels documentés sont passés de 226 en 2023 à 245 en 2024 (+7,75 %), atteignant 290 décès notifiés à la semaine 56 de 2025 (+20 %). De manière cruciale, huit zones de santé clés représentent plus de 60 % de tous les décès maternels provinciaux. Selon la stratégie 2026 du Cluster Santé en RDC, 7,5 millions de personnes ont besoin d'une assistance sanitaire à l'échelle nationale, avec un financement prioritaire ciblant 1,7 million de personnes vulnérables, dont 425 000 femmes en âge de procréer.

**Portée de l'évaluation et méthodologie**

Une évaluation rapide de la réponse et des capacités de préparation en santé sexuelle et reproductive (SSR) a été menée par le Groupe de travail SSR Nord-Kivu entre avril et mai 2026 dans 10 zones de santé ciblées : Mweso, Masisi, Birambizo, Bambo, Rutshuru, Kibirizi, Binza, Beni, Butembo et Katwa. Coordonnée par les autorités sanitaires et les partenaires humanitaires, l'évaluation a porté sur 42 établissements de santé. Elle a utilisé une méthodologie mixte, quantitative et qualitative, intégrant des observations directes des structures, des revues de registres médicaux, des entretiens avec des informateurs clés parmi le personnel soignant et des discussions de groupe au sein des communautés.

**Lacunes opérationnelles des structures et déficits d'approvisionnement**

L'évaluation a révélé de dures pénuries de ressources humaines et des goulots d'étranglement opérationnels dans les structures de santé. Seuls 5 des 42 établissements évalués disposent d'un médecin spécialiste en gynécologie-obstétrique, tous concentrés dans les centres urbains (Butembo et Katwa), laissant les hôpitaux généraux de référence (HGR) ruraux totalement dépourvus de spécialistes. Bien que 35 structures offrent des soins obstétriques et néonatals d'urgence de base (SONUB), des ruptures de stock critiques affectent fréquemment les anticonvulsivants (sulfate de magnésium), les kits d'aspiration manuelle par intra-utérine (AMI) et les extracteurs sous vide. Plus de 60 % du personnel de maternité n'a reçu aucune formation continue en SONUB au cours des trois dernières années, l'HGR de Nyamilima signalant un écart de neuf ans depuis sa dernière formation. De plus, plus de 45 % des structures font face à des ruptures de stock récurrentes de kits post-viol pour les survivantes de violences basées sur le genre (VBG), et seulement 12 % proposent des services de SSR adaptés aux jeunes.

**Obstacles à l'accès communautaire et difficultés financières**

Les retours de la communauté ont mis en évidence de severes obstacles économiques, physiques et sécuritaires pour accéder aux soins de SSR. Plus de 78 % des usagers paient de leur poche pour les soins de maternité, un accouchement simple coûtant entre 25 000 et 60 000 francs congolais (environ 10 à 23 USD) et les césariennes atteignant 150 000 FC (environ 60 à 65 USD). Les systèmes de référence d'urgence sont gravement défaillants : 76 % des transferts d'urgence se font à moto-taxi et 63 % à pied ou sur des brancards, tandis que les ambulances fonctionnelles ne représentent que 13 % des transports. Dans plus de 82 % des références, les familles paient elles-mêmes les frais de transport (15 à 50 USD), ce qui entraîne des retards fatals. La perception de la sécurité lors des déplacements nocturnes chute en dessous de 15 % en raison de la présence de groupes armés actifs.

**Priorités stratégiques (6 axes d'action)**

Pour stabiliser les résultats en matière de santé sexuelle et reproductive (SSR), le rapport établit six axes prioritaires stratégiques dans les zones de santé clés, tels qu'intégrés dans le Plan de réponse à la mortalité maternelle et périnatale évitable :

1. **Soins obstétriques d'urgence** : Déployer des équipes médicales mobiles dans les HGR ruraux et fournir des formations accélérées en SONUB et AMI.
2. **Chaînes d'approvisionnement en produits de santé** : Assurer un approvisionnement ininterrompu en kits d'urgence de santé reproductive de l'UNFPA (1 à 12) et sécuriser les produits de transfusion sanguine provinciaux.
3. **Accessibilité financière** : Appliquer la gratuité des services de maternité, de césarienne et de planification familiale pour les populations vulnérables.
4. **Transport médicalisé** : Mettre à disposition des ambulances 4x4 pour les HGR et prendre en charge intégralement les frais de transfert d'urgence.
5. **Réponse aux VBG et aux jeunes** : Sécuriser les stocks de kits post-viol de 72 heures, recruter des assistants psychosociaux et aménager des espaces adaptés aux jeunes.
6. **Surveillance communautaire et redevabilité** : Soutenir les relais communautaires (RECO), installer des boîtes à idées et rendre obligatoires les audits de décès maternels dans le DHIS2.

*\[English version\]*

**Executive Context and Assessment Overview**

The eastern region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), particularly Nord-Kivu province, faces an acute humanitarian crisis driven by armed conflict and severe population displacement involving over 2.5 million internally displaced persons (IDPs). This volatile environment has caused a sharp increase in maternal mortality across the province. Documented maternal deaths rose from 226 in 2023 to 245 in 2024 (+7.75%), reaching 290 notified deaths by week 56 of 2025 (+20%). Crucially, eight key health zones account for over 60% of all provincial maternal deaths. Under the DRC Health Cluster 2026 Strategy, 7.5 million people require health assistance nationwide, with critical priority funding targeting 1.7 million vulnerable individuals, including 425,000 women of reproductive age.

**Assessment Scope and Methodology**

A rapid evaluation of the Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) response and preparedness capacity was conducted by the SRH Working Group North Kivu between April and May 2026 across 10 targeted health zones: Mweso, Masisi, Birambizo, Bambo, Rutshuru, Kibirizi, Binza, Beni, Butembo, and Katwa. Coordinated by health authorities and humanitarian partners, the assessment evaluated 42 healthcare facilities. It utilized a mixed quantitative and qualitative methodology incorporating direct facility observations, medical register reviews, key informant interviews with healthcare workers, and community focus group discussions.

**Facility Operational Gaps and Supply Deficits**

The assessment revealed severe human resource shortages and operational bottlenecks across health facilities. Only 5 out of 42 evaluated facilities have a specialist Obstetrician-Gynecologist, all concentrated in urban centers (Butembo and Katwa), leaving rural General Reference Hospitals (HGR) entirely without specialists. Although 35 facilities offer Basic Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal Care (BEmONC), critical stockouts frequently affect anticonvulsants (magnesium sulfate), manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) kits, and vacuum extractors. Over 60% of maternity staff received no continuous BEmONC training in the last three years, with Nyamilima HGR reporting a gap of nine years since its last training. Furthermore, over 45% of facilities face recurring stockouts of Post-Rape kits for Gender-Based Violence (GBV) survivors, and only 12% offer youth-adapted SRH services.

**Community Access Barriers and Financial Hardships**

Community feedback highlighted severe economic, physical, and security barriers to receiving SRH care. Over 78% of service users pay out-of-pocket for maternity care, with an uncomplicated delivery costing between 25,000 and 60,000 Congolese Francs (approximately $10–$23) and C-sections reaching 150,000 FC (approximately $60–$65). Emergency referral systems are severely impaired: 76% of emergency transfers rely on motorcycle taxis and 63% on foot or stretchers, while functional ambulances account for only 13%. In over 82% of referrals, families personally pay transport costs ($15–$50), leading to fatal delays. Nighttime travel security perception drops below 15% due to active armed groups.

**Strategic Priorities (6 Action Axes)**

To stabilize sexual and reproductive health (SRH) outcomes, the report establishes six strategic priority axes across key health zones, as incorporated into the Response Plan for Preventable Maternal and Perinatal Mortality:

1. **Emergency Obstetric Care**: Deploy mobile medical teams to rural HGRs and provide accelerated BEmONC and MVA training.
2. **Commodity Supply Chains**: Ensure uninterrupted supplies of UNFPA Emergency Reproductive Health Kits (1–12) and secure provincial blood transfusion products.
3. **Financial Accessibility**: Enforce free maternity, C-section, and family planning services for vulnerable populations.
4. **Medicalized Transport**: Provide 4x4 ambulances to HGRs and fully cover emergency transfer costs.
5. **GBV and Youth Response**: Secure 72-hour Post rape kit stocks, recruit psychosocial assistants, and establish youth spaces.
6. **Community Surveillance and Accountability**: Support community health worker

Sur ce total, 24 alertes ont fait l'objet d'évaluations, permettant d'identifier 110 besoins humanitaires affectant plusieurs secteurs essentiels. Les incidents signalés ont touché environ 70 500 personnes, dont 36 600 ont été identifiées comme ayant besoin d'une assistance humanitaire. Par ailleurs, 38 200 personnes ont reçu une assistance, à travers 60 interventions humanitaires. Parmi les personnes affectées figurent environ 12 000 personnes déplacées internes vivant sur des sites, 2 000 déplacés hébergés dans des familles d’accueil et 155 retournés. fields.title: Safe and dignified burials help prevent the spread of Ebola
fields.body:
**Bunia, Democratic Republic of the Congo**—In Ituri Province, in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, safe and dignified burials play a critical role in the fight against Ebola. The disease spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, and after death, certain burial practices can expose family members to the virus if appropriate protective measures are not in place. In a region where funeral rites are central to community life, protecting families while respecting traditions remains essential.

When the current outbreak began in the province, health teams were met with considerable mistrust in some communities. “In the beginning, many people did not understand why health teams needed to intervene during burials,” explains Pastor Richard Ndjaridjo. Some families hesitated to report deaths and continued to organize funerals on their own. In some cases, bodies that had already been buried were exhumed to allow relatives to carry out certain traditional rites. Teams responsible for safe and dignified burials also faced threats and attacks, complicating efforts to stop the spread of the virus. In this context, developing an approach that protected communities while respecting their beliefs and cultural practices became a priority.

To address these challenges, the Ministry of Health, with support from the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners, implemented a community engagement approach. Through the Standby Partners mechanism, Paul Benjamin Gbadia was deployed to WHO to support the Ebola response in Ituri. Faced with the difficulties encountered by safe and dignified burials teams during the early stages of the outbreak, he helped strengthen an approach that placed communities at the centre of the response. Working alongside health authorities and partners, he helped train and mentor local volunteers so they could participate directly in safe and dignified burial activities.

“We found that communities were more willing to accept safe and dignified burials when they were directly involved in the response,” he explains. “By engaging local volunteers, we were able to establish closer dialogue with families and better address their concerns.”

In Jina, in Djugu Territory, 36 community members were trained and assigned to safe and dignified burial and decontamination teams. Comprised of people known and trusted by residents, these teams support families while applying the measures needed to prevent Ebola transmission. For Paul, the goal was to make communities active participants in the response rather than passive beneficiaries. “Local volunteers speak the language, understand the customs and know the concerns of their communities. This closeness makes dialogue easier and helps build acceptance of prevention measures,” says Gbadia.

Over time, this approach helped strengthen trust between communities and health teams. Recalling a recent death in Jina, Naema Mave, a member of a safe and dignified burial team, describes how the family immediately alerted health authorities and waited for the team to arrive before proceeding with the burial. “When we arrived, no one had touched the body. A few months earlier, that might not have been the case,” she explains.

For Mave, this progress reflects the value of the training and support provided to local volunteers, enabling them to respond safely and independently within their communities.

Ndjaridjo also attributes this change to sustained community awareness efforts. “There has been a lot of sensitization. People have come to understand that bodies can transmit the disease and they now accept the intervention of safe and dignified burial teams to protect families,” he says.

Beyond training community teams, WHO has provided technical, logistical and operational support to safe and dignified burial activities. This support includes personal protective equipment, essential operational supplies, transportation to reach remote areas and ongoing field mentoring for teams.

Since the start of the response, and as of 27 September 2026, more than 11 573 alerts have been recorded, 10 357 safe and dignified burials conducted in Ituri and 9 433 laboratory samples collected and tested. Twenty safe and dignified burial teams, including 10 mobile teams and 10 community-based teams, have received operational, logistical and training support. These results highlight the importance of a trust-based approach.

“When communities participate directly in safe and dignified burial activities, they take greater ownership of prevention measures. This has helped reduce resistance and better protect families,” says Gbadia.

According to Dr Danny Byaruhanga, Medical Director of Jina, community involvement has strengthened the response. “We can say that safe and dignified burial teams have played a major role in interrupting transmission within the community. Once families accepted that burials could be carried out by trained and properly equipped personnel, it significantly reduced the risks associated with handling bodies,” he explains.

Beyond its immediate impact on preventing Ebola transmission, this approach is also helping communities build their capacity to respond to future public health emergencies. By encouraging participation and ownership of prevention activities, it promotes the adoption of protective practices and behaviours that can continue long after the current outbreak has ended.

In Ituri, experience has shown that safe and dignified burials rely as much on trust as on protective measures. When a family reports a death, accepts support from a trained team and takes part in prevention efforts, a high-risk situation can become an opportunity to protect an entire community.

fields.title: European Union supports Tearfund Netherlands in responding to impact of conflict in the Central African Republic
fields.body:
Utrecht, 9th of October 2026 – Communities in the Lim-Pendé prefecture in the North-West of the Central African Republic (CAR) continue to face the consequences of years of conflict, displacement and underinvestment in basic services. Many schools lack adequate classrooms, safe water and sanitation facilities, while vulnerable families struggle to access essential services. Through European Union humanitarian funding, Tearfund Netherlands is helping to improve access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, while supporting safe and inclusive learning environments for children in conflict-affected communities.

 The response forms part of a wider humanitarian programme led by Plan International in Lim-Pendé prefecture. Within this programme, Tearfund is responsible for delivering WASH activities in partnership with the local organisation RHIBES. The intervention will improve access to safe drinking water, sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion for approximately 12,000 people across some of the most vulnerable communities in the sub-prefecture of Ndim.

 ‘The European Union remains committed to supporting people affected by humanitarian crises in the Central African Republic, where conflict and displacement continue to undermine access to essential services, including education, water and sanitation,’ said Jean-Paul Jemmy Ghomsi, Head of the EU Humanitarian Aid office in Bangui. ‘Through our humanitarian funding, we help ensure that vulnerable communities can access safe drinking water, hygiene services and quality education, while strengthening their resilience and protecting their dignity.’

 Needs assessments conducted in the target area revealed severe gaps in basic WASH services. Many communities rely on unsafe water sources, a large number of boreholes are non-functional, and sanitation facilities are either absent or inadequate. Schools are particularly affected, with limited access to water points and hygienic latrines, creating additional barriers to education, especially for girls and children with disabilities.

 Under the project, Tearfund will construct and rehabilitate 17 water points, including solar-powered systems and hand-pump boreholes, improve sanitation facilities in schools and communities, establish water management committees, and promote sustainable hygiene practices through community-led awareness activities. The programme is designed to ensure long-term community ownership and maintenance of the infrastructure.

 ‘Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene is fundamental for health, protection and education,’ said Martin Herlaar, Director International Programs of Tearfund Netherlands. ‘With support from the European Union, Tearfund is working alongside communities and local partners to restore essential services and help create a safer and healthier environment for children and families affected by conflict.’

 The EU-funded programme is expected to reach more than 22,000 people through integrated education, child protection and WASH interventions. By combining improvements in school infrastructure, access to education, child protection measures and safe water services, the action aims to strengthen the resilience of communities and improve opportunities for children living in one of the country's most vulnerable regions.

 **About Tearfund Netherlands**

 Tearfund Netherlands is part of the global Tearfund family. Together, we work with local partners to tackle poverty, respond to disasters and challenge injustice in more than 50 countries worldwide. Through locally led approaches, Tearfund supports communities affected by conflict, climate change and vulnerability to build resilient and sustainable futures.

 For more information, please contact info@tearfund.nl.

 **About EU Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid**

 The European Union and its Member States are the world's leading donor of humanitarian aid.

 Relief assistance is an expression of European solidarity with people in need all around the world. It aims to save lives, prevent and alleviate human suffering, and safeguard the integrity and human dignity of populations affected by natural disasters and man-made crises.

 Through its Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations DG ECHO, the European Union helps millions of victims of conflict and disasters every year. With headquarters in Brussels and a global network of field offices, the EU provides assistance to the most vulnerable people on the basis of humanitarian needs.

 For more information, please contact Anouk.Delafortrie@echofield.eu.

fields.title: Tchad : Evaluation territoriale et Plan de relèvement local d’Adré - Octobre 2026
fields.body:
**RESUME EXECUTIF**

Frontalière du Darfour, la sous-préfecture d’Adré est l’une des zones de l’est du Tchad les plus affectées par la crise soudanaise, avec 214 943 réfugiés enregistrés à la date du 14 septembre 2026,1 et une place parmi les dix premières zones accueillant des retournés vulnérables en juillet 2026.2 Les informations disponibles y restaient fragmentées et peu centrées sur l’ensemble des groupes de populations – déplacés et non-déplacés – présents à l’échelle territoriale. Pour y remédier, une évaluation territoriale (ABA) a été conduite dans le cadre de l’initiative AGORA, financée par l’Agence Française pour le Développement (AFD), avec l’implication du Comité Mixte de Gouvernance Territoriale (CMGT) mis en place par la même initiative, afin d’appuyer la planification locale et l’élaboration d’une feuille de route opérationnelle dénommée Plan de Relèvement Local (PRL).

L’évaluation couvre la Ville d’Adré, le site d’accueil temporaire (SAT) et 42 villages situés dans un rayon d’environ 20 km. Elle combine des données quantitatives et qualitatives collectées d’avril à août 2026 avec une composante d’analyse géospatiale transversale : cartographie des infrastructures et des cartographies participatives, analyses d’accessibilité aux services, télédétection (occupation du sol, stress de la végétation), modélisation des zones inondables et tendances climatiques sur 30 ans. Elle permet de spatialiser les résultats et d’ancrer les priorités du PRL dans le territoire. Les résultats ménages sont représentatifs pour les non-déplacés et les retournés de la Ville et pour les réfugiés du SAT ; ils sont indicatifs pour les réfugiés en Ville, comme les données rurales, qualitatives et issues des gestionnaires. fields.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo Country Report: The State Of the Humanitarian System 2026
fields.body:
**EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

This country report for the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) provides an evidence-based overview of the current international humanitarian system between 2022 and 2025 to supplement the global analysis in [The State of the Humanitarian System 2026 (SOHS)](https://alnap.org/sohs/). It describes the country’s humanitarian context and responses to ongoing crises; outlines the size, shape and performance of the humanitarian system; and highlights key findings from primary research in North and South Kivu, supplemented with secondary data including scholarly and grey literature. The country report offers a comprehensive picture of how the international humanitarian system, alongside other actors, operates in DRC and it assesses the system’s effectiveness in meeting the needs of people affected by conflict and crises.

Our research indicates a mixed picture of the state of the humanitarian system in DRC, with several important challenges. Improvements include better delivery of aid in line with internationally recognised standards in more accessible areas, as well as greater preparedness and capacity among skilled staff to respond to the needs of populations affected by crisis. Humanitarian actors are also increasingly adapting their operational approaches to better support community needs. However, several structural challenges continue to hinder the effectiveness of the humanitarian system in DRC. The system remains heavily dominated by United Nations (UN) agencies and international organisations, who control funding, resources and agenda-setting processes, often to the detriment of local and national actors, as well as people affected by crisis. Other challenges include access, ensuring accountability to affected people, and widespread sexual abuse and exploitation.

The power imbalance between international and local actors – with international actors holding a near-monopoly over decision-making power – combined with limited government engagement, creates an environment in which humanitarian actors operate with excessive autonomy and a laissez-faire, hands-off approach. This situation is further reinforced by a lack of transparency, weak accountability mechanisms, political influence and insufficient action to address other forms of misconduct. There remains limited progress on localisation, and practices such as gatekeeping continue to negatively affect adherence to humanitarian principles. In this context, some aid workers exploit these systemic weaknesses to engage in corrupt practices, diversion of humanitarian assistance and other forms of misconduct, including sexual exploitation and abuse and other practices that undermine the dignity of aid recipients.

Corruption and aid diversion take many forms and represent some of the most critical setbacks in the humanitarian system in eastern DRC. They are both structural and systemic, sometimes involving well-organised networks and actors who are supposed to prevent and combat these excesses. Together, these challenges undermine the effectiveness of humanitarian interventions and erode the sector’s overall credibility and trustworthiness.

Organisations have adapted through local partnerships and by modifying modalities, but assistance has not met needs. Prioritisation has focused narrowly on survival, leaving critical sectors such as protection and psychosocial support underserved.

At the household level, aid has been inconsistent and poorly adapted to prolonged displacement, with uneven targeting and the exclusion of vulnerable groups. Consequently, trust has declined, resource competition has increased and social tensions have grown.

**Recommendations**

Decision-makers, humanitarian stakeholders and practitioners need to promote good practices of humanitarian assistance. This includes:

- developing mechanisms that promote transparency and social accountability in all steps of assistance, including verification mechanisms that specifically target local chiefs and aid camps in coordination with aid frontline staff
- promoting protection and dignity, including preventing and combating sexual exploitation and abuse
- working to shift decision-making power to national and local humanitarian actors, as well as para-humanitarian stakeholders
- proactive preparedness for epidemics and outbreaks
- prioritising services in collaboration with local communities, where replacement funds cannot be secured.

fields.title: Central African Republic - Key Message Update: Crisis persists in conflict-affected areas despite the gradual end of the lean season, September 2026 - January 2027
fields.body:
**Key Messages**

- **Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist through January 2027 in the areas most affected by insecurity and isolation, particularly Vakaga, Haute-Kotto, Haut-Mbomou, as well as parts of the northwest.** Despite the seasonal improvement expected from October onward in the north, below-average production and livelihoods constrained by insecurity, high prices, and low purchasing power will continue to limit food access. Clashes, displacement, mobility restrictions, and tensions related to [**transhumance**](https://www.journaldebangui.com/rca-pres-de-2-700-personnes-deplacees-apres-le-meurtre-dun-eleveur-a-batangafo/) will continue to disrupt agricultural activities, livelihoods, and access to markets. Households will increasingly resort to reducing the number of meals, taking on debt, and selling assets to meet their food needs. In contrast, in Bamingui-Bangoran, the decline in conflict-related incidents and improved access to fields and forest resources are expected to support an improvement to Stressed (IPC Phase 2) in October.
- **From September through January 2027, Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected to continue to predominate in several prefectures in the central, southern, and southwestern parts of the country, particularly Ouaka, Basse-Kotto, and Nana-Mambéré.** In these relatively more stable areas, maize and groundnut harvests, which have been underway since August, are gradually improving food availability and reducing households’ reliance on markets. Cassava, which is available year-round, also contributes to food access. In addition, income from seasonal agricultural activities supports the livelihoods of poor households. Most of these households are expected to be able to meet their essential food needs without heavy reliance on negative coping strategies. However, in Haut-Mbomou, persistent insecurity continues to limit access to fields, hunting, fishing, and gathering, exposing the most affected households to more severe difficulties in accessing food and income.
- **Agroclimatic conditions observed during the first 10 days of September remain favorable for crop development across most of the country.** Cumulative rainfall observed since the beginning of the season has generally been average to above average, with [**localized deficits**](https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/Early_Estimates/v3/Recent_Rainfall/observed/moving_18pentad/africa_west/pngs/archive/POA_18PentAccum_2026_p50.png) in the northeast, northwest, and southeast. In the central and southern areas, maize, groundnut, and rice harvesting has already begun or is nearing completion following the August/September start and generally satisfactory growing conditions. In the north, millet and sorghum crops are continuing to mature, and the main harvests are expected from October onward. Production prospects remain generally average in relatively stable areas, in line with estimates from the [**Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)**](https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country/CAF/pdf/CAF.pdf). However, limited access to agricultural inputs, as well as localized security constraints, will continue to restrict production levels in some affected areas.
- **Prices of major cereals remained high in August, particularly in isolated areas and areas affected by insecurity in the northeast.** In August, the price of maize in Birao (514 FCFA/kilogram) was approximately twice as high as in Bangui (257 FCFA/kilogram), reflecting [**persistent supply constraints**](https://reliefweb.int/report/central-african-republic/republique-centrafricaine-initiative-conjointe-de-suivi-des-marches-icsm-aout-septembre-2026?utm_source=rw-subscriptions&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=country_updates_54) and high transportation costs. Continued [**fuel shortages**](https://www.journaldebangui.com/rca-bangui-confrontee-a-une-nouvelle-penurie-de-carburant/) in September are expected to disrupt market supplies and trade flows, contributing to persistently high transportation costs and higher prices for imported food commodities. However, ongoing maize, groundnut, and rice harvests in several areas of the central, western, and southern parts of the country are expected to gradually improve market supplies and contribute to a seasonal decline in prices in relatively stable areas. In contrast, difficulties accessing markets in areas affected by insecurity and isolation are expected to keep prices relatively high.

fields.title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 4, 23 July-23 September 2026
fields.body:
**Highlights**

- The outbreak continues to expand geographically. Laboratory-confirmed cholera cases are reported in twenty-one health districts across the Far North and North regions, while four additional districts in the Far North remain under investigation for suspected cases.
- UNICEF is supporting the Government-led response through Health, WASH, Social and Behaviour Change, Accountability to Affected Populations, Child Protection, Nutrition, Youth Engagement and coordination.
- The response is 48 per cent funded. A US$660,800 gap remains, with particularly significant needs in Health, Nutrition and Child Protection/MHPSS.

**Overview**

Cholera transmission continues to expand across the Far North and North regions. Population movements and active transmission in neighbouring areas increase the risk of further spread. Immediate priorities include stronger surveillance, timely case management, targeted WASH interventions, risk communication and preparedness in affected and high-risk districts.

As of 23 September 2026, the Far North region has reported 2,753 cholera cases and 77 deaths (CFR: 2.8%), with active transmission persisting in several health districts, notably Mada, Kolofata, Mokolo, Mora and Makary. The implementation of two rounds of reactive Oral Cholera Vaccination (OCV) campaigns in seven high-risk districts (Fotokol, Kousseri, Mada, Makary, Mora, Kolofata and Mokolo) has likely contributed to reducing the spread and severity of the outbreak. However, the worsening humanitarian situation, including population displacement from Logone-et-Chari division due to insecurity, is placing additional pressure on host communities in Waza and the urban health districts of Maroua I, Maroua II and Maroua III. This influx of displaced populations is increasing vulnerability to cholera transmission through overcrowding and heightened pressure on already constrained health and WASH services.

In the North Region, 37 cases and 6 deaths have been reported (CFR: 16.22%). Guider reported the highest number of cases. Although the caseload remains low, the high case fatality rate may indicate delays in detection and referral or limited access to quality case management.

Continued surveillance, WASH interventions, risk communication and community engagement and cross-border coordination remain critical to prevent further spread and reduce mortality

fields.title: Disease Outbreak News: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, Democratic Republic of the Congo (8 October 2026)
fields.body:
**Situation at a glance**

On 5 October 2026, WHO was informed about a laboratory-confirmed imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) in Kenya with travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Kenya through Uganda. The patient was hospitalized and treated in Kenya but subsequently died on 5 October. Public health response measures have been initiated in Kenya and Uganda, including contact tracing. Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 25 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded to one additional health zone, Alimbongo health zone in North Kivu, adding to the geographic footprint of an outbreak that remains concentrated in the eastern part of the country. As of 6 October 2026, the country has recorded 8728 confirmed cases and 4205 confirmed deaths, corresponding to a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.2%. The cases have been reported from 64 health zones across seven provinces out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. At the national level, transmission remains intense, although the burden is unevenly distributed. In some areas, there are clear signs that the epidemic is slowing down, although in others it continues to grow. Over the past three completed epidemiological weeks, new weekly cases nationwide have increased by 2.5% from 475 to 487, while new weekly deaths remain stable at 224 compared to 222. The persistently high mortality, together with the large number of deaths occurring outside treatment centres, continues to point to delays in identifying illness and reaching appropriate care. Since the last Disease Outbreak News, 264 of the 372 reported deaths occurred in communities and 108 in treatment centres. On 1 October, the Netherlands reported the medical evacuation of a healthcare worker who tested positive by PCR for Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. At the time of reporting, the patient has been undergoing treatment in the Netherlands.

**Description of the situation**

Since the previous [Disease Outbreak News](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON618) was published on 25 September 2026, an additional 775 confirmed cases, including 379 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In the most recent 24-hour period, as of 6 October, 62 new confirmed cases were reported, with Ituri accounting for 33 cases and North Kivu for 30. No new cases were reported in Bas-Uélé, South Kivu or Sud-Ubangi during that period. Across the preceding seven days, the average number of new cases rose to 72 per day.

As of 6 October, cumulative confirmed cases have reached 8728, including 4205 deaths and 2269 recoveries. The overall crude CFR is 48.2%.

Confirmed cases have now been identified in 64 health zones across seven provinces. Forty-eight of the 64 affected zones reported at least one new case during the preceding 21 days, while 16 reported no recent cases. Ituri remains the most extensively affected province, with 28 of 36 health zones reporting cases during this outbreak, followed by North Kivu (17/34), Haut-Uélé (7/13), Tshopo (7/23), Bas-Uélé (3/11), South Kivu (1/34) and Sud-Ubangi (1/16). Alimbongo in North Kivu is the most recently affected health zone and reported four confirmed cases, including two deaths.

Ituri remains the epicentre, with 6480 cumulative confirmed cases and 2989 deaths. North Kivu follows with 1755 confirmed cases and 1013 deaths, and continues to record the highest provincial CFR, at 57.7%. Haut-Uélé has reported 364 cases and 153 deaths, while Tshopo has recorded 51 cases and 17 deaths. The less-affected provinces continue to report substantially fewer cases, but transmission persists in several of them. The most affected health zones were Beni and Katwa in North Kivu, and Rwampara, Bunia and Mandima in Ituri. The continued occurrence of cases across multiple provinces shows that the outbreak remains geographically active even as intensity varies between health zones.

Contact follow-up remains a major operational pressure and has fluctuated below the response target in recent weeks. Coverage was 87.6% on 16 September, briefly above the target of 85%, but fell to 74.7% by 25 September. Although coverage subsequently improved to 82.0% on 27 September, it remained below target and stood at 80.4% in the latest reporting period, with 23 741 of 29 535 contacts reached as of 4 October. The current level therefore reflects a persistent gap in the ability to monitor exposed people consistently throughout the 21-day follow-up period.

**Kenya**

On 6 October 2026, the Ministry of Health of Kenya reported the first laboratory-confirmed imported case of BVD in Kenya.

According to an official statement from the Ministry of Health, the individual is an adult who lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient became ill approximately one month ago and was treated in several hospitals while in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Kampala, Uganda, by road before arriving in Nairobi, Kenya by air on 3 October. It is currently unclear if and when he was symptomatic during these travels, but upon arriving ill in Kenya, the patient was transported by a relative directly to Nairobi Hospital and isolated in the facility. A sample collected from the patient on 5 October was positive for BDBV at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute Laboratory on the same day. The patient was given supportive treatment but subsequently died.

A safe and dignified burial has been conducted. Public health response actions were immediately initiated. Contact tracing is ongoing, including for the international flight.

Given the timelines of the illness, and the one month time from initial symptoms to death, it is presumed he was not initially sick with BVD, which does not usually have such a long progression from infection to symptoms and death, but became infected with BVD in a health facility or community while seeking care for another ailment.

**The Netherlands**

On 1 October 2026, the Netherlands reported the medical evacuation of a healthcare worker who tested positive by PCR for BDBV in the Democratic Republic of the Congo where the patient was working on the Ebola disease outbreak response. Following confirmation of the diagnosis, the patient was safely repatriated to the Netherlands under strict medical and infection-prevention procedures, in close coordination with the relevant health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Netherlands. As with previous medically evacuated cases, this case will not be reported as a local case of BVD in the Netherlands.

**Epidemiology**

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the *Orthoebolavirus species*. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to initially occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are inadequate, and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

The CFR from the previous two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification and investigation, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through the health areas with active transmission.

**Public health response**

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: [Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa](https://www.afro.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease/outbreak-drc-26)

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures, including disease surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, research, logistics and support for response interventions and essential health services, engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

**WHO risk assessment**

On 14 August 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the outbreak of BVD, incorporating newly available information on the evolving situation. The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was separated from the risk for other countries in the African Region.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as very high, the risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as high, and the risks for the rest of the African region and at the global level was again assessed as low.

A detailed rapid risk assessment is currently ongoing to assess the risk in Kenya and will be reported once available.

**WHO advice**

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event.

The updated [Temporary Recommendations](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-08-2026-second-meeting-of-the-ihr-emergency-committee-on-the-epidemic-of-ebola-bundibugyo-virus-disease-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-temporary-recommendations) issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.
